body.problem: The insrc workflow produces an artifact at each stage that a human must review and approve before the next stage may proceed, and it also surfaces open questions the reviewer is expected to settle at that moment. For a developer working inside a JetBrains IDE, none of that review-and-approve moment is reachable where they work. There is no in-IDE way to notice that an artifact is waiting for approval, to read it in a legible rendered form, to annotate specific parts of it with feedback, to record decisions against its open questions, or to give the approval that unlocks the next stage. To do any of this the developer must leave the IDE and drive the workflow from an external surface, breaking their flow at exactly the human-in-the-loop gate the workflow most depends on — so in practice the review either happens out-of-band or is skimmed. The feedback a reviewer forms while reading is not captured against the artifact in any structured way from the IDE, so it is not carried into the stage that consumes it, and the reviewer cannot even tell from inside the IDE which artifacts are currently pending. The cost lands squarely on the JetBrains developer population the in-IDE integration was built to serve, at the one step of the workflow that by design cannot be automated away.

nonGoals.text: A general-purpose diff or pull-request review tool over arbitrary source files.
nonGoals.rationale: The surface is scoped to workflow artifacts awaiting approval; code review is already a separate, distinct workflow stage.

nonGoals.text: Real-time push notification of newly-produced artifacts via a daemon event or subscription stream.
nonGoals.rationale: Approval is a human, non-latency-critical action; a bounded pending-discovery mechanism suffices and avoids standing up new streaming infrastructure on both the daemon and plugin sides. Deferred to a possible later enhancement.

nonGoals.text: Moving approval or open-question-resolution logic into the plugin.
nonGoals.rationale: The plugin must stay a thin orchestrator that owns no reasoning; the daemon remains the single owner of the approve gate and the resolution machinery [[c1]].

nonGoals.text: Editing or authoring the artifact body from within the review surface.
nonGoals.rationale: Artifact content is produced by the workflow stages; the reviewer annotates and resolves questions, and a single artifact stays the single source of truth [[c5]].

nonGoals.text: A multi-user or collaborative review (multiple reviewers, cross-user comment threads, presence).
nonGoals.rationale: This Epic targets the single developer reviewing in their own IDE; multi-party review is a separate concern.

nonGoals.text: Guaranteeing the rich review experience on IDE runtimes that lack the embedded-browser capability.
nonGoals.rationale: Those setups get a graceful fallback rather than the rich surface; making them first-class would compromise the primary experience [[c6]].

assumptions.text: Reviewers approve artifacts as a deliberate human action that is not latency-critical, so a bounded pending-discovery mechanism (rather than instantaneous push) is acceptable.
The embedded-browser capability is present in the standard bundled runtime of all four target IDEs, with only a small fraction of setups (an alternative runtime) needing the fallback path.
The existing daemon approve and artifact-read contracts and the open-question resolution machinery are stable surfaces this Epic can build on without redesigning them.
The plugin's existing local-socket client is sufficient transport for the request/response calls this surface needs.
The artifacts a reviewer needs to act on are discoverable by their persisted approval state (approved vs pending vs rejected).

constraints.text: The plugin must remain a thin orchestrator that owns no reasoning: it may render and transport, but approval and open-question-resolution logic stay in the daemon.
All daemon access from the plugin goes over the existing local Unix-domain-socket JSON-RPC channel; the plugin opens no cloud or REST path.
Approval must flow through the existing approve path that stamps the artifact's approved state and honours the review block-verdict gate; the surface must not stamp approval by any other route.
Reviewer feedback must be recorded through the existing open-question resolution machinery so the next stage's start-gate consumes it, not through a parallel side-channel comment store.
A single artifact remains the single source of truth; the surface renders the artifact's existing rendered content and never creates a divergent second copy of it.

The one plugin artifact must continue to load and activate across all four target IDEs off the shared platform module, and the review surface must degrade gracefully wherever the embedded-browser capability is unavailable.
Pending-artifact discovery must impose no unbounded always-on background load; it must be a bounded, on-demand or polled read rather than a hot loop.

stories.title: See which artifacts are waiting for approval, from inside the IDE
stories.userValue: A reviewer can tell at a glance, without leaving the IDE, which of the open project's workflow artifacts are currently awaiting their approval.

acceptanceCriteria.given: the open project has workflow artifacts in mixed states — some already approved, some awaiting approval, some rejected
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer asks the IDE what needs review
acceptanceCriteria.then: only the artifacts that are awaiting approval (neither approved nor rejected) are listed, each identified by what it is

acceptanceCriteria.given: the backing service cannot be reached
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer asks the IDE what needs review
acceptanceCriteria.then: the IDE reports that the backing service is unavailable rather than presenting an empty list as though nothing were pending

acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer asks the IDE what needs review
acceptanceCriteria.then: the IDE clearly indicates nothing is currently awaiting review

localConstraints.text: Determining what is pending must be a bounded, on-demand or periodic check, never a continuous hot loop that burdens the IDE or the backing service.

stories.title: Open a pending artifact and read it rendered legibly in the IDE
stories.userValue: A reviewer can read the full artifact in a legible, rendered form inside the IDE, instead of opening a terminal to see it.

acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer opens it in the IDE
acceptanceCriteria.then: its content is shown in a rendered, legible form within the IDE

acceptanceCriteria.given: an IDE runtime that lacks the rich in-IDE rendering capability
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer opens a pending artifact
acceptanceCriteria.then: it still opens in a readable fallback view that carries the same review actions

acceptanceCriteria.given: an artifact is displayed for review
acceptanceCriteria.then: what is shown is exactly the artifact's own content, with no separately-maintained second copy that could diverge from it

localConstraints.text: The content presented for review is the artifact's own rendered form; the surface never authors or stores a divergent second copy of the artifact body.
Where the rich in-IDE renderer is unavailable, the surface degrades to a plain readable view rather than failing to open.

stories.title: Annotate specific parts of an artifact with inline comments
stories.userValue: A reviewer can attach feedback to the exact place in the artifact it concerns, the way they would in a code review, rather than describing it out of band.

acceptanceCriteria.given: an artifact is open for review
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer selects a specific part of it and adds a comment
acceptanceCriteria.then: the comment is shown anchored to that part

acceptanceCriteria.given: several comments have been added to different parts of the artifact
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer looks over their annotations
acceptanceCriteria.then: each comment is distinctly associated with the part it targets

acceptanceCriteria.given: a comment has been added but not yet submitted
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer edits or removes it
acceptanceCriteria.then: the change is reflected before anything is submitted

localConstraints.text: Un-submitted annotation state is presentation-only inside the IDE; the surface performs no approval or resolution reasoning of its own.

stories.title: Submit annotations so they are recorded against the artifact and carried into the next stage
stories.userValue: The feedback a reviewer captured is durably recorded where the next stage will act on it, instead of being lost in chat or a scratch note.

acceptanceCriteria.given: one or more annotations on an artifact awaiting approval
acceptanceCriteria.then: they are recorded against that artifact through the workflow's own feedback mechanism so the next stage consumes them
it is stored by the backing service, not in a separate side-channel maintained only by the IDE

acceptanceCriteria.given: the backing service cannot record a submission
acceptanceCriteria.then: the IDE reports the failure and the annotations are not silently dropped

localConstraints.text: Reviewer feedback is recorded only through the workflow's existing open-question resolution mechanism, never a parallel comment store.

stories.title: Approve a pending artifact from the IDE, unlocking the next stage
stories.userValue: A reviewer can give the approval that advances the workflow without leaving the IDE.

acceptanceCriteria.given: an artifact awaiting approval is open in the IDE
acceptanceCriteria.then: it is approved through the workflow's existing approve path and its state becomes approved

acceptanceCriteria.given: an artifact whose review verdict blocks approval
acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer approves it without an explicit override
acceptanceCriteria.then: approval is withheld and the reason is shown, matching the workflow's own gate

acceptanceCriteria.when: the reviewer returns to the list of what needs review
acceptanceCriteria.then: the just-approved artifact no longer appears as pending

localConstraints.text: Approval is effected only through the existing approve path that stamps approval and honours the review block-verdict gate; the surface never marks an artifact approved by any other route.

citations.quotedText: The JetBrains plugin is a thin config-orchestrator that owns no reasoning; this Epic adds an in-IDE review/approve surface on top of it.
'workflow.approve' (:555), 'artifact.get' (:980), 'artifact.search' (:994) are the registered daemon IPCs; approve + read exist, but no list-pending or submit-comment method does.
approveWorkflowTarget(req, opts?) stamps meta.approvedAt and honours the review block-verdict — the existing approve path.
The plugin already has a one-shot local Unix-domain-socket JSON-RPC client (UnixSocketDaemonRpc/DaemonGateway) that opens only the local socket, never a cloud/REST path.
The open-question resolution machinery (recordResolution) and the single-source artifact renderers exist; there is no user-comment-submission IPC and no divergent second copy of an artifact body.
The embedded browser is core platform API bundled with the runtime across IntelliJ-Platform IDEs; check availability before use and provide a fallback when the IDE runs a runtime without it.
The only file watcher is the indexer's source watcher; the socket supports per-request streaming but there is no artifact/approval event emitter, so discovery is a bounded polled read.
